title: Cyclin-CDK Control of the Cell Cycle

generated.pipeline: extract → Opus draft → Sonnet accuracy gate → Sonnet fixes

cards.front: In a cyclin-CDK complex, the CDK is the {{c1::catalytic}} subunit, and it is inactive alone.
cards.back: The cyclin is the regulatory subunit that switches it on and steers it to targets.
cards.quote: CDKs (cyclin-dependent kinases) are the catalytic subunits, and they are inactive alone.
cards.section: The engine: a kinase and a partner that comes and goes

cards.front: In a cell cycle with strong brake control, such as an early frog embryo, how does the mitotic kinase activity trace differ from the cyclin trace?
cards.back: Cyclin climbs steadily through interphase and drops at division (a sawtooth). Kinase activity stays low most of interphase, can snap up abruptly just before mitosis, and crashes as cyclin is destroyed.
cards.quote: It stays low through most of interphase, can snap up abruptly just before mitosis, and crashes as cyclin is destroyed.
cards.section: The record: a sawtooth and a snap

cards.front: At the metaphase-to-anaphase transition, which two proteins does the APC/C tag for destruction, and what does losing each one do?
cards.back: Securin: the sister chromatids separate. Cyclin B: CDK activity falls and the cell can leave mitosis.
cards.quote: tags two targets for destruction: securin, so the sister chromatids separate, and cyclin B, so activity falls and the cell can leave mitosis.
cards.section: The record: a sawtooth and a snap

cards.front: In mammals, which cyclin and which CDK usually act at the G1/S transition?
cards.back: Cyclin E with CDK2.
cards.why: In mammals cyclin D-CDK4/6 acts in G1, cyclin A-CDK2 in S, and cyclins A and B with CDK1 in G2 and M. This is the usual division of labour, not a strict requirement.
cards.quote: Different cyclin-CDK pairs carry the rise through different stretches of the cycle.
cards.section: The engine: a kinase and a partner that comes and goes

cards.front: MPF (maturation-promoting factor), the activity that makes frog oocytes mature, is CDK1 bound to {{c1::cyclin B}}.
cards.back: CDK1 was first named Cdc2, from fission yeast.
cards.quote: is CDK1 (first named Cdc2, from fission yeast) bound to cyclin B.
cards.section: The engine: a kinase and a partner that comes and goes

cards.front: Name the four conditions CDK1 needs at once to be active.
cards.back: A cyclin bound; an activating phosphate added by CAK (CDK-activating kinase); no inhibitory phosphates (from Wee1, and Myt1 in animal cells); no inhibitor protein bound.
cards.quote: To be active, CDK1 needs four things at once: a cyclin bound; an activating phosphate, which a CDK-activating kinase (CAK) adds to a loop near the active site
cards.section: Holding the rise back, and letting it go

cards.front: The kinase {{c1::Wee1}} puts an inhibitory phosphate on CDK1 at tyrosine 15; the phosphatase Cdc25 removes it.
cards.back: Wee1 is the brake; Cdc25 is its release.
cards.quote: The names to hold on to are the brake, Wee1, and its release, Cdc25; the rest is detail.
cards.section: Holding the rise back, and letting it go

cards.front: Cyclin B rises steadily through G2. Why does CDK1 activity lag behind instead of rising with it?
cards.back: Wee1 phosphorylates each new CDK1-cyclin B complex as it forms, so inactive complexes pile up, loaded and waiting, until Cdc25 removes the phosphates.
cards.quote: All through G2, Wee1 keeps phosphorylating the new CDK1-cyclin B complexes as they form, so inactive complexes pile up, loaded and waiting.
cards.section: Holding the rise back, and letting it go

cards.front: Why does CDK1 activity snap on all at once at mitotic entry instead of creeping up?
cards.back: Active CDK1 phosphorylates Cdc25 (more active) and Wee1 (less active). These two positive feedback loops mean each active complex frees more, so activation is all or none.
cards.quote: These two positive loops mean each active complex frees more, so activity does not creep up; it snaps, all or none.
cards.section: Holding the rise back, and letting it go

cards.front: Around G1/S in mammalian cells, how is the CDK inhibitor p27 removed so cyclin E-CDK2 can switch fully on?
cards.back: Cyclin E-CDK2 phosphorylates p27, the SCF ubiquitin ligase tags it, and the proteasome destroys it.
cards.why: p21 and p27 block CDK2 and CDK1 complexes by binding, without any chemistry, so destroying the inhibitor removes the brake. Sic1 is the yeast counterpart.
cards.quote: Around G1/S, cyclin E-CDK2 phosphorylates p27, the SCF ubiquitin ligase tags it for the proteasome
cards.section: Holding the rise back, and letting it go

cards.front: A fission-yeast cell is engineered to make much more Cdc25 than normal. Predict when it divides and at what size.
cards.back: Earlier and smaller. More phosphatase removes the inhibitory phosphate before the cell reaches its usual size, so CDK1 snaps on early and the cell enters mitosis small.
cards.why: Losing Wee1 gives the same result, which is how wee1 got its name.
cards.quote: With more of the phosphatase, the brake comes off before the cell reaches its usual size, CDK1 snaps on early, and the cell enters mitosis small.
cards.section: Holding the rise back, and letting it go

cards.front: A fission-yeast cell loses Cdc25 activity in G2. Predict what happens to CDK1 and to mitotic entry.
cards.back: CDK1-cyclin B complexes keep the inhibitory phosphate Wee1 added, so CDK1 stays off and the cell does not enter mitosis.
cards.why: Rule: Cdc25 is the release for the Wee1 brake; without it, loaded complexes pile up but never switch on.
cards.quote: The phosphatase Cdc25 takes the phosphates off and releases them
cards.section: Holding the rise back, and letting it go

cards.front: In Xenopus egg extracts with protein synthesis blocked, entry into mitosis needs about 32 to 40 nM of nondegradable cyclin B, and a mitotic extract stays mitotic down to about 16 to 24 nM. Two extracts get 28 nM: one starts in interphase, one already in mitosis. Predict each.
cards.back: The interphase extract stays in interphase (below the entry threshold); the mitotic extract stays in mitosis (above the stay threshold).
cards.why: Rule: the Cdc25 and Wee1 feedback loops give the switch memory, so less cyclin is needed to stay in mitosis than to enter. The numbers belong to that assay.
cards.quote: Two thresholds with a gap between them are the mark of a switch with memory
cards.section: The extract thresholds

cards.front: The G1 decision to divide is the {{c1::restriction point}} (in yeast, Start), passed only with enough nutrients and growth factors.
cards.quote: That decision is the restriction point (in yeast, Start), and a cell passes it only if it has enough nutrients and growth factors.
cards.section: A decision in G1

cards.front: How do growth-factor signals lead to S-phase gene expression through Rb and E2F?
cards.back: Growth signals raise cyclin D; cyclin D-CDK4/6 phosphorylates Rb, which releases E2F. E2F switches on S-phase genes, including cyclin E, and cyclin E-CDK2 phosphorylates Rb further.
cards.quote: Cyclin D-CDK4/6 begins to phosphorylate Rb, a protein that holds the E2F transcription factors off.
cards.section: A decision in G1

cards.front: Growth factors are removed from a mammalian cell shortly after it has passed the restriction point. Predict what it does, in the classical model.
cards.back: It finishes the cycle anyway.
cards.why: The Rb-E2F loop is a switch: cyclin E-CDK2, made because of E2F, keeps phosphorylating Rb, so once flipped it no longer needs the growth signal.
cards.quote: once it flips, the cell finishes the cycle even if the growth factors are taken away
cards.section: A decision in G1

cards.front: A mammalian cell makes an Rb that cyclin-CDK complexes cannot phosphorylate. Growth factors are plentiful. Predict whether it enters S phase.
cards.back: It stays in G1. Rb keeps holding E2F off, so S-phase genes, including cyclin E, are not switched on and the cell does not pass the restriction point.
cards.quote: Freed E2F switches on genes for S phase, including cyclin E, and cyclin E-CDK2 phosphorylates Rb further.
cards.section: A decision in G1

cards.front: How does DNA damage in G1 hold a mammalian cell in G1?
cards.back: p53 builds up and switches on the gene for p21; p21 binds and blocks CDK2 complexes, so the cell waits in G1.
cards.quote: p53 builds up and switches on the gene for p21. p21 binds and blocks CDK2 complexes, and the cell waits in G1.
cards.section: Checkpoints pull the same levers

cards.front: How does damaged or unfinished DNA in G2 keep a cell out of mitosis?
cards.back: ATM and ATR, through Chk1 and Chk2, inactivate Cdc25 (and Chk1 activates Wee1), so CDK1 keeps its inhibitory phosphate and the cell waits in G2.
cards.quote: The sensor kinases ATM and ATR, through Chk1 and Chk2, inactivate Cdc25 (and Chk1 activates Wee1)
cards.section: Checkpoints pull the same levers

cards.front: How does the spindle assembly checkpoint delay anaphase?
cards.back: Unattached kinetochores switch it on, and it stops the APC/C and its partner Cdc20 from destroying securin and cyclin B, so the cell waits before anaphase, often in prometaphase.
cards.quote: It stops the APC/C and its partner Cdc20 from destroying securin and cyclin B, so the cell waits before anaphase, often in prometaphase.
cards.section: Checkpoints pull the same levers

cards.front: Mammalian cells lacking p53 are irradiated in G1. Predict what happens to them.
cards.back: The lasting G1 stop fails: without the main burst of p21, many enter S phase with damaged DNA. They can still be stopped later, at the G2 checkpoint, which acts through Cdc25 and Wee1.
cards.quote: They lose the main burst of p21, so the lasting G1 stop fails and many enter S phase with damaged DNA.
cards.section: Checkpoints pull the same levers

cards.front: A drug keeps microtubules from attaching to kinetochores in dividing mammalian cells. Predict the levels of securin and cyclin B, and where the cells stop.
cards.back: Securin and cyclin B stay high, and the cells wait before anaphase, often in prometaphase.
cards.why: Unattached kinetochores keep the spindle assembly checkpoint on, which blocks APC/C-Cdc20 from destroying securin and cyclin B.
cards.quote: Unattached kinetochores, the sites where chromosomes grip the spindle, switch on the spindle assembly checkpoint.
cards.section: Checkpoints pull the same levers

cards.front: What does separase do at anaphase, and what holds it off until then?
cards.back: Separase cuts cohesin, the protein ring holding sister chromatids together. Securin holds it off until the APC/C tags securin for destruction.
cards.quote: Losing securin frees separase, the enzyme that cuts cohesin, the protein ring holding sister chromatids together
cards.section: The fall: destruction makes it one way

cards.front: After mitosis, the APC/C with {{c1::Cdh1}} keeps mitotic cyclins low through G1, so CDK activity starts the next cycle from the bottom.
cards.back: In mitosis the APC/C works with Cdc20 instead.
cards.quote: Then the APC/C with Cdh1 keeps mitotic cyclins low through G1, so activity starts the next cycle from the bottom.
cards.section: The fall: destruction makes it one way

cards.front: Why does destroying cyclin, rather than switching CDK1 off, make the exit from mitosis one way?
cards.back: Removing a phosphate, releasing an inhibitor or silencing a checkpoint can be reversed. A destroyed protein cannot be switched back on; it has to be made again.
cards.quote: A destroyed protein cannot be switched back on; it has to be made again.
cards.section: The fall: destruction makes it one way

cards.front: Vertebrate cells in mitosis cannot destroy cyclin B. A CDK1 inhibitor is added briefly, the cells start to leave mitosis, and then the drug is washed out. Predict what happens.
cards.back: They go back toward mitosis. Cyclin B was never destroyed, so CDK1 switched back on once the drug was gone; after a short treatment, low activity alone was only a pause.
cards.quote: Cyclin B was never destroyed, so once the drug was gone CDK1 switched back on.
cards.section: The fall: destruction makes it one way

cards.front: A cell makes a securin that the APC/C cannot tag, while cyclin B is destroyed normally. Predict what happens to the sister chromatids.
cards.back: They fail to separate. Securin keeps separase off, so cohesin is not cut, even though cyclin B is destroyed.
cards.why: Rule: the APC/C tags two targets with two separate results; securin destruction is what frees separase.
cards.quote: Once kinetochore checkpoint signaling has been silenced, the APC/C with Cdc20 tags securin and cyclin B.
cards.section: The fall: destruction makes it one way

cards.front: What is origin licensing, and when in the cycle can it happen?
cards.back: Loading the helicase that will later unwind the DNA onto an origin. It happens only while CDK activity is low, in late mitosis and G1.
cards.quote: Licensing happens only while CDK activity is low, in late mitosis and G1.
cards.section: Copy once: low activity licenses, high activity fires

cards.front: How does the CDK cycle make each replication origin fire at most once per cycle?
cards.back: Origins are licensed only while CDK activity is low; firing needs S-phase CDK activity (with DDK); high activity from S to mitosis blocks relicensing in yeast and contributes to blocking it in animal cells, which add other locks (geminin, Cdt1 destruction). New licences wait until activity falls again.
cards.quote: Firing a licensed origin needs S-phase CDK activity, together with a second kinase, DDK.
cards.section: Copy once: low activity licenses, high activity fires

cards.front: Fission-yeast cells overproduce the CDK inhibitor Rum1, so CDK activity falls without a mitosis. Predict what happens to their DNA.
cards.back: They copy it again, running through repeated S phases without dividing.
cards.why: Rule: low activity licenses origins afresh, and when activity rises again they fire. Cells lacking the mitotic B-cyclin Cdc13 do the same.
cards.quote: With activity low, the origins are licensed afresh; when activity rises, they fire, and the cells run through repeated S phases without dividing.
cards.section: Copy once: low activity licenses, high activity fires

cards.front: Cultured HeLa cells from different phases are fused so two nuclei share one cytoplasm. A G1 nucleus fused with an S-phase cell starts replicating early; a G2 nucleus does not. What two conclusions follow?
cards.back: S-phase cytoplasm carries an activity that can start replication (it fires origins the G1 nucleus has licensed). Under these fusion conditions a G2 nucleus does not start another round, because its fired origins cannot be licensed again until CDK activity falls.
cards.quote: a G1 nucleus in a cell fused with an S-phase cell started replicating early, while a G2 nucleus in the same situation did not.
cards.section: Copy once: low activity licenses, high activity fires

cards.front: A mitotic mammalian cell is fused with a G1 cell. Predict what happens to the G1 nucleus.
cards.back: It condenses its chromosomes prematurely.
cards.why: Mitotic cytoplasm is dominant: it is full of active CDK1-cyclin B, which with the kinases and phosphatases it controls can condense an interphase nucleus from G1, S or G2.
cards.quote: Mitotic cytoplasm is dominant: it is full of active CDK1-cyclin B
cards.section: Copy once: low activity licenses, high activity fires

cards.front: In a cell-fusion test of whether S-phase cytoplasm drives replication in G1 and G2 nuclei, what controls are needed, and what can the method not tell you?
cards.back: Same-phase fusions (G1 with G1 and G2 with G2 test whether fusion itself starts replication; S with S tests whether fusion blocks it) and unfused neighbours on the same slide. Fusion identifies an activity and a nuclear competence, not the molecules.
cards.quote: Limit: fusion identifies an activity and a nuclear competence, not the molecules.
cards.section: Design problem

cards.front: A cell exits mitosis but cannot switch on APC/C-Cdh1, so mitotic cyclins stay present and CDK activity never falls to its low level in G1. Predict what happens to origin licensing and the next S phase.
cards.back: Origins would not be newly licensed, so few or no origins could fire in the next S phase.
cards.why: Rules: APC/C-Cdh1 keeps mitotic cyclins low through G1, and licensing happens only while CDK activity is low.
cards.quote: Before an origin of replication can fire, it must be licensed: loaded with the helicase that will later unwind the DNA there.
cards.section: Copy once: low activity licenses, high activity fires

cards.front: What did Masui and Markert's 1971 frog oocyte experiment show, and how was it done?
cards.back: Cytoplasm from progesterone-treated oocytes injected into untreated oocytes made them mature. It revealed an activity, maturation-promoting factor (MPF), not a molecule.
cards.quote: Like cell fusion, this revealed an activity, not a molecule.
cards.section: How the engine was found: frogs, yeast and sea urchins

cards.front: For a temperature-sensitive cdc mutant, what is the execution point, and how does it differ from the arrest point?
cards.back: The execution point is the last time in the cycle the gene's function is needed. The arrest (termination) point is where cells collect when the function fails.
cards.quote: The station is the execution point: the last time in the cycle the gene's function is needed.
cards.section: How the engine was found: frogs, yeast and sea urchins

cards.front: A budding-yeast cdc mutant's gene has its execution point in G1, but cells arrest with large buds. At the shift to the restrictive temperature, one cell is in S phase with a small bud. Where does it stop?
cards.back: It finishes this cycle, divides, and stops in the next cycle with a large bud.
cards.why: Rule: a cell already past the execution point completes the current cycle; it fails at the gene's step next time and collects at the arrest point.
cards.quote: If the station closes just after the car has filled up, it finishes this lap and stalls on the next
cards.section: How the engine was found: frogs, yeast and sea urchins

cards.front: What is the DNA content of a diploid cell in G1, and in G2 and M?
cards.back: 2C in G1; 4C in G2 and M. One C is the DNA of one haploid genome. A G2 cell is still diploid.
cards.quote: One C is the DNA of one haploid genome, so a diploid cell has 2C in G1 and 4C in G2 and M.
cards.section: Measuring the states

cards.front: Which cell-cycle states can a propidium iodide DNA-content histogram alone not separate, and why?
cards.back: G0 from G1, and M from G2. Each pair has the same DNA content: G0 and G1 sit in the 2C peak, and G2 and mitotic cells in the 4C peak.
cards.quote: G0 cells sit in the 2C peak with G1, and mitotic cells sit in the 4C peak with G2.
cards.section: Measuring the states

cards.front: What does a short EdU pulse mark in a cell population, and how is it detected?
cards.back: Cells in S phase: EdU, a thymidine analogue, is built into DNA made during the pulse and then detected by click chemistry with a fluorescent tag.
cards.quote: EdU, a thymidine analogue, is built into DNA made during a short pulse and is then detected by click chemistry with a fluorescent tag
cards.section: Measuring the states

cards.front: Why is phospho-histone H3 (serine 10) close to a mitotic marker but not an exact one?
cards.back: It marks condensing mitotic chromosomes, but the mark begins in late G2 and is removed from anaphase on.
cards.quote: It is close to a mitotic marker but not exact: the mark begins in late G2 and is removed from anaphase on.
cards.section: Measuring the states

cards.front: In an exponentially growing culture, why does multiplying a phase's cell fraction by the doubling time overestimate how long G1 lasts?
cards.back: Each division turns one old cell into two newborns, so the culture always holds twice as many cells just born as cells about to divide. Early phases are overrepresented.
cards.quote: Each division turns one old cell into two newborn ones, so a growing culture always holds twice as many cells just born as cells about to divide.
cards.section: Worked problem: fractions are not durations

cards.front: An asynchronous diploid culture doubles every 30 h; every cell is cycling and none die. 40% of cells are in the 2C peak. Using t = -T log2(1 - F/2), how long does G1 last?
cards.quote: Step 3, solve for t: 2^(−t/T) = 1 − F/2, so t = −T × log2(1 − F/2).
cards.section: Worked problem: fractions are not durations

cards.front: The same culture (doubling time 30 h, all cycling, none dying) has 40% of cells at 2C, 30% between the peaks (S) and 30% at 4C. Using t = -T log2(1 - F/2), how long do G2 plus M last, and how does that compare with the naive estimate?
cards.back: End of S: F = 0.70, t = -30 x log2(0.65) = 18.64 h. G2 plus M = 30 - 18.64 = 11.36 h, longer than the naive 0.30 x 30 = 9.0 h.
cards.why: In this model the last phase always looks shorter than it is, because cells about to divide are underrepresented.
cards.quote: In this model the first phase, G1, always looks longer than it is and the last, G2 plus M, shorter
cards.section: Worked problem: fractions are not durations

cards.front: A culture used for phase-duration estimates actually has many resting G0 cells. Predict how this distorts the estimated G1 duration from a DNA histogram, and why.
cards.back: G1 is likely overestimated. G0 cells sit in the 2C peak with G1, inflating the G1 fraction, and the formula assumes no resting cells, so the G1 estimate is unreliable.
cards.quote: The model assumes identical phase lengths in every cell and no resting or dying cells, so treat these as estimates.
cards.section: Worked problem: fractions are not durations

cards.front: Asynchronous cultures of p53-normal and p53-null cells are irradiated, and DNA histograms are taken some hours later. Predict how the 2C and 4C peaks differ between them.
cards.back: p53-normal cells hold many cells in the 2C (G1) peak. p53-null cells lose the lasting G1 stop but can still be held at the G2 checkpoint (acting through Cdc25 and Wee1), so a 4C accumulation is expected, not guaranteed.
cards.why: Rules: the G1 stop needs p53 and p21; the G2 checkpoint acts through Cdc25 and Wee1 without p53; G2 cells have 4C DNA.
cards.quote: Other damage responses can delay them briefly, and they can still be stopped later, at the G2 checkpoint, which acts through Cdc25 and Wee1.
cards.section: Checkpoints pull the same levers
